Lens Click a card · fix · watch it move

I. The warning

I was nine the spring the river came up through Hollins. We kids were sent to the church hall, where Mara Okafor counted us at the door. I remember her pencil more than the water.

We would argue that the archive was never neutral. I spent two winters in it, and the warnings are filed in the order they were answered, not the order they were sent.

II. The town

As we'll see, the order matters. Hollins had two sirens and one man who knew how to work both. When he drove north to check the levee, the south siren stayed quiet.

Every family lost something that spring. The ones on the north bank lost the most, and theirs are the accounts the archive kept.

III. The ledger

Mara kept the church ledger: names, times, what was carried in. Here we must admit the record is thin, but it is honest about being thin.

Our view is that the ledger, not the archive, holds the town's memory. I have read it more times than I can count, and on every page Hollis reads like a smaller town than the one I grew up in.

You're right, I'd narrowed it to sentences. I've reworked `docs/writing-instruments.md` around six levels (word, sentence, paragraph, section, piece, collection). Above the sentence level, the new pieces are:

- **Consistency ledgers.** Code finds every occurrence of something across the piece, and Jev judges only the ambiguous ones. They cover I/we stance, narrating tense, point of view within a scene, spelling of names, terminology drift, and a copyeditor's style sheet. Each one can be fixed one at a time or all at once, or marked **Deliberate**. Deliberate adds a Charter rule, so the ledger stops flagging the mix but still catches new drift.
- **Characters and entities.** Every character is tracked across sections, so you can see who drops out and where. The doc also covers relationships and how their tension changes chapter by chapter, and continuity checks for details like a character's age or a coat that changes colour.
  - One test I think is new: hide who is speaking and ask Jev to guess the speaker of each line. If Mara's lines keep getting attributed to Tom, the two characters sound alike.
- **Structure.** Outline headings get small markers for share of the piece, open problems and score. Each promise the piece makes is tracked as kept, open or dropped. Pacing curves run alongside the outline.

## The living score

The prototype above is clickable, but its numbers are scripted, not real model output. It's saved at `tmp/living-desk.html`.

The rubric can't do this today. It asks Jev for one score per criterion over the whole draft, and only reviews drafts of 500+ words, at most once every 30 seconds after a save. So the grade can't point to where it comes from, and it can't move while you edit.

The proposal updates at three speeds:

- **Instantly, in code:** counts, the style sheet, and the static features. `scoreStaticFeatures` already exists; it's just only called at review time.
- **When a paragraph settles:** Jev rescores that paragraph against the criteria a paragraph can show, like evidence, integrity, pacing and voice.
- **Periodically:** a full-piece read rescores criteria like thesis and structure, and confirms the estimate.

Each card's impact is roughly the criterion's weight × the gap to the next score level × how much of the piece is affected. Cards are ordered by impact, so the one that matters most comes first.

One untested assumption: I don't yet know whether rolling paragraph scores up into a grade matches what a whole-piece read gives. That's why the estimate is marked ≈ and is replaced by the confirmed full read when it arrives. We'd need to check it on real drafts before the estimate can be trusted.

## Next step

I've re-ordered the phases. Phase 1 is now the "living skeleton":

- the common card shape;
- the document spine beside the page;
- the lens system that highlights one problem across the manuscript;
- live static scoring;
- the code-only ledgers: style sheet, name variants, I/we counts, and who appears where.

All of it works offline. The I/we ledger classified by Jev comes right after, in Phase 2. Should I start building Phase 1 in the editor?

# Living desk: design guidance

Companion to `docs/writing-instruments.md`. This governs how the living desk looks, moves, and speaks. The contract is `src/utils/living-desk-contract.ts`.

## What it should feel like

A copyeditor's style sheet and a proofreader's pencil, not a dashboard. The writer should feel the piece being *watched over*, never *graded at*. Three tests decide every detail:

1. **Cause and effect are visible.** Every fix produces three linked reactions at once: the span in the manuscript, the card's count, and the score. If any one of the three is missing, the moment feels fake.
2. **The manuscript stays the hero.** The desk recolours the page; it never covers it. Nothing animates while the writer types.
3. **Nothing is claimed that wasn't measured.** Estimates carry ≈. Model classifications carry their probability. Rule findings say "by rule".

## Spatial logic

- **Left is the piece; right is the passage.** The right margin already holds passage notes (flow rail, in-flow tools). The desk and the spine sit on the left, beside the outline, because they are about the whole document.
- **Panel:** a fixed aside on the left, in the same slot as the outline panel (`top: 5rem; bottom: 4rem; left: 1rem; width: 20rem`). Opening one closes the other. Below 64rem viewport width it becomes a bottom sheet capped at 55vh.
- **Spine:** a 6px strip hugging the page's left edge for the full height of the manuscript. It widens to 12px on hover or focus. Section boundaries are hairlines; occurrences of the active lens are ticks; the focused finding's ticks are full strength and the rest are 35%. The top of the spine carries a small score cap (the estimate, tabular figures) that opens the panel.
- **Hidden when quiet:** no spine in manual Zen, in automatic flow (`html[data-flow]`), or in read-only mode without findings. The desk never reveals itself while the writer types: it can update counts, but it only *opens* on request.

## Visual language

Use the existing tokens only; every theme (foolscap, broadsheet, nightpress) must work without overrides.

| Element | Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Panel | `--color-paper` background, 1px `--color-paper-3` border, `border-radius: 2px`, the same shadow as `.in-flow-card`. No rounded SaaS corners, no gradients. |
| Section heads in the panel | `.dept-label` (typewriter, uppercase, 0.32em tracking, `--color-ink-muted`). |

**Lens colours (flagged / context):**

| Lens | Flagged | Context |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stance | `--color-vermilion` underline 2px + `--color-highlight-rose` wash | `--color-cobalt` text weight 600 for "I" |
| Naming | `--color-mustard` wavy underline | `--color-highlight-sky` wash on canonical spelling |
| Style | `--color-text-periwinkle` dotted underline | none |
| Presence | per-entity wash from the persona palette (cobalt, sage, periwinkle, mustard, blush) at 35% | none |

Colour is never the only signal: flagged spans always carry an underline style, and cards say what the colour means in words.

## Manuscript decorations

The engine adds these classes; the interface styles them globally (decorations live inside ProseMirror's DOM).

- `.ld-occ` on every decorated span, with `data-ld-lens` and `data-ld-label`.
- `.ld-occ--flagged`, `.ld-occ--context`, `.ld-occ--focused` (the focused finding), `.ld-occ--previewing` (original text shown struck through during a preview).
- `.ld-ghost` widget immediately after a previewed span: the replacement in italic `--color-accent-green`, with a 1px dashed left rule. It must not shift line breaks more than the replacement itself would.
- `.ld-flash` for 1.2s after a fix lands: `--color-highlight-mint` fading to transparent.
- The editor root gets `data-ld-lens="<lens>"` while a lens is on and `data-ld-focus` while a finding is focused. **Only `data-ld-focus` dims** the rest of the text (to `--color-ink-light`, not lighter); a lens alone just marks occurrences. The dim lifts the moment the caret enters the manuscript and a key is pressed.

## Motion

- Score number: tween 600ms, ease-out cubic. Criterion bar width: 700ms `cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1)`; the fill turns `--color-accent-green` for 2.4s after a rise, `--color-accent-amber` after a fall.
- Delta flag: a small pill beside the criterion (`+0.3 · ¶6`) that fades in over 200ms, holds 2.4s, then fades out.
- **No reordering under the pointer.** When a finding resolves or its impact changes, keep the list order until the pointer leaves the list (or 1.5s with no pointer), then reflow with a 200ms FLIP. A card the writer is working in never moves.
- Resolved cards drop to 60% opacity with a ✓ and move to the end on the next reflow.
- `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: no tweens, flashes or FLIP; values change instantly and the delta pill stays static for the same duration.

## Copy

- Name observable things: "3 editorial “we” · 41 “I”", "“Hollis” once in ¶6, “Hollins” 14 times". Never "you seem unsure", never "AI suggests".
- Buttons name the action: "Make it I", "Make all 3 I", "Use “Hollins”", "The mix is deliberate", "Hollis is a different place". Not "Apply", "Accept", "OK".
- Impact: "≈ +0.27". Below 0.05 show "small". Null impact shows the criterion name instead.
- Provenance: "rule", "Jev .88", "model". When judgement is unreachable, a single "rule-only" chip at the top of the panel, with the tooltip "No judgement model reachable, so classifications are by rule."
- Empty: "Nothing across the piece needs you right now." followed by one muted line listing what is watched: "Watching stance, names and the style sheet."
- Short drafts (under about 150 words): "The desk starts reading at about 150 words."
- Deliberate: "Kept on purpose. Twyne will flag only new drift."

## States each card must handle

open · improving (some fixed) · resolved · deliberate · stale (the span moved; show "This changed since it was found" and disable its fix) · read-only (no fix buttons; jump only) · judgement pending (a quiet "reading…" in the metric line, never a spinner).

## Accessibility

- Panel: `<aside aria-label="The piece">`. Each card header is a `<button aria-expanded>`. Fix buttons are real buttons with text labels.
- One polite live region announces score changes: "Consistency up 0.3 after the fix in paragraph 6."
- Keyboard: Escape clears focus and the lens, then closes the panel. Enter on an occurrence row jumps to it. Focus returns to the card after a fix, never to the manuscript.
- Spine ticks are decorative (`aria-hidden`); the same jumps are reachable from the cards.

## Anti-patterns

- Rounded, glossy cards, coloured gradients, emoji, or icons where a word fits.
- Toasts for routine fixes. The reaction belongs where the change happened.
- A score that moves while the writer types prose. Rule criteria may recompute on every edit, but the estimate's *animation* runs only after a fix or a 2s pause.
- A grade shown without saying whether it is confirmed or estimated.
- Opening the panel automatically.

## Acceptance checks

1. Open the desk on a draft with a mixed I/we stance. Fix one occurrence. Within 300ms: the span flashes, the count drops by one, the consistency bar rises with a delta pill naming the paragraph, and the estimate tweens with ≈.
2. Press Undo. Everything returns, including the count and the estimate.
3. Mark the stance finding deliberate, reload: it stays deliberate.
4. Switch theme to nightpress: every lens colour is legible (WCAG AA against the page for text, 3:1 for underlines).
5. Type a paragraph with the panel open: nothing animates, nothing reorders, typing latency is unchanged.

Both agents are now building Phase 1 in parallel:

- **Engine:** Codex on GPT-6.1-Sol, high reasoning, Fast tier.
- **Interface:** Sonnet 5.5 on low.

Before handing off, I wrote three things myself.

**The shared contract** (`src/utils/living-desk-contract.ts`). It's the only thing the two halves share, so neither has to wait for the other. It defines:
- what a finding and an occurrence look like;
- the live score;
- the controller the interface calls (`applyFix`, `applyAll`, `preview`, `markDeliberate`, `jumpTo`, `confirm`);
- the events the engine sends out.

**The design guidance** (`docs/living-desk-design.md`). It's built around three tests:
1. Every fix visibly changes three things together: the text, the card's count, and the score.
2. The manuscript stays central; nothing animates while you type.
3. Nothing claims more than was measured: estimates show ≈, model labels show their probability.

The rest is concrete:
- the piece-level desk and the spine sit on the left; the right margin stays for notes on single passages;
- only your existing paper and ink colour tokens and typefaces, with an assigned colour per lens;
- timings for animations and a rule that cards never reorder under your pointer;
- button labels name the action ("Make it I", "Hollis is a different place");
- accessibility requirements, things to avoid, and five acceptance checks.

**File ownership.** Each agent has a list of files it may edit. Codex makes only two small edits to the editor itself: one start call and one extension registration. Neither agent will commit or touch anything else in your uncommitted work.

What Phase 1 covers:
- **Engine (Codex):**
  - *I/we stance:* code finds the obvious cases, Jev classifies the ambiguous ones, and the fix adjusts the verb ("we were" → "I was").
  - *Name spellings:* catches variants like "Hollins" vs "Hollis".
  - *Style sheet:* serial comma, US vs UK spelling, numbers as digits or words, dash spacing, curly vs straight quotes.
  - *Presence:* tracks where each name appears across sections.
  - *Live score:* rule-based criteria that update on every edit, a "consistency" criterion, and an estimate built on the last confirmed review.
  - *Stance without a Convex sign-in:* the stance check calls Jev even without a Convex client. This removes a gate the audit flagged, but only for this feature.
- **Interface (Sonnet):**
  - the "The piece" panel and the document spine;
  - lens highlighting in the manuscript, with ghost-text previews;
  - Storybook stories built on the flood-memoir example;
  - a toggle on the Review toolbar.

When both finish, I'll review the code against the contract and the design spec, check that the two halves connect, run the tests and type checks, and test it in the running editor. Then I'll report back.
